events.objective: Establish the symptom timeline and true blast radius for the login latency/503 incident. Determine: exact onset time of auth-service p99 degradation and 503s on /v1/auth/login (was it gradual or step-change?); whether other services are also degraded at the same time (latency, error rates, saturation) even if not reported; whether dependencies of auth-service (DB, cache, downstream services) show resource or latency anomalies; and the error signature of the 503s (timeouts, connection pool exhaustion, upstream refused, etc.). Report onset timestamp and the full set of affected services with their metric trends.

Build the change and dependency picture across ALL services around the incident window. List all deployments and config changes (any service, not just auth-service) from ~2026-04-21 through 2026-04-22T08:59Z with timestamps; map auth-service's upstream/downstream dependencies and any shared components (shared cache, DB, auth library); and search historical incidents for the prior bcrypt regression (what its signature and root cause were) plus any other similar login-slowdown precedents. Report which changes plausibly precede the onset and whether the incident pattern matches a code release, a config change, or a shared-infrastructure event.

Correlate the change/dependency findings from task b against the onset time found in task a. Specifically test whether latency/errors in auth-service are explained by its own behavior (CPU saturation, bcrypt-like high CPU on login path) versus an external dependency (DB/connection pool, shared cache) by comparing auth-service CPU/memory/latency metrics on the login path with the resource trends of its dependencies at the exact onset time. Confirm or rule out the bcrypt-regression hypothesis and identify which entity moved first.

args.query: bcrypt regression login latency auth-service release
503 login timeouts cache miss storm shared redis database saturation
auth-service config change feature flag log level deployment

events.statement: Across ALL services, the only deployment in the window 2026-04-21T00:00Z to 2026-04-22T08:59Z was dep-5803 on portfolio-service (v4.4.0, 'Holdings export', CSV export endpoint) at 2026-04-22T05:50:00Z, status 'live', rolled_back_at null. No deployment of auth-service or any auth-related service occurred in this window.
A wider look-back (2026-04-14T00:00Z to 2026-04-21T00:00Z) returned zero deployments for all services, so no release precedes the onset in the week before the incident either.

The only config change in the window was cfg-2801 on auth-service: key 'log.level' changed INFO -> WARN at 2026-04-22T03:40:00Z by config-bot, described as 'Reduce log volume'. It affects logging verbosity only, not auth logic or bcrypt parameters.

auth-service dependency edges: auth-service -> user-db (kind 'db'), auth-service -> redis-cache (kind 'cache'), auth-service -> kyc-provider (kind 'external', has_telemetry false); api-gateway -> auth-service (http). user-db and redis-cache are owned by 'platform'.

redis-cache is a SHARED component ("shared":true) used as a cache by four services: auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service. portfolio-service -- the only service that deployed in the window -- is one of redis-cache's callers.

Historical precedent HIST-101 (2025-08-14, 'Login latency after auth-service release'): symptoms 'login p99 4s' and '503 on login' with 'high cpu', root cause 'bcrypt cost factor raised 10->14 in release v6.4.0', category bad_deployment, resolution 'Rolled back v6.4.0'. The current symptom set (auth p99 3.8s, 503 on /v1/auth/login) is nearly identical, but that past cause was a deployment and no auth-service deployment exists in the current window. Other auth precedents are HIST-109 (JWT clock-skew default -> 401s) and HIST-108 (JWKS key rotation -> 401s), both 401/invalid_token signatures, not latency/503.

events.answer: No code release and no meaningful config change precedes the onset on auth-service or any dependency: the only deployment in the whole window is portfolio-service v4.4.0 at 2026-04-22T05:50Z (unrelated CSV export), and the only config change is auth-service log.level INFO->WARN at 03:40Z (log volume only). The symptom set is nearly identical to the HIST-101 bcrypt regression (p99 4s, 503 on login, high CPU), but that precedent's cause was a deployment and no auth-service deployment exists now, so the pattern does NOT match a code release; it matches either a shared-infrastructure event (redis-cache is shared and also used by the just-deployed portfolio-service) or an as-yet-unseen cause rather than the bcrypt release the reporter guessed.

events.statement: auth-service p99 latency was a flat ~90 ms baseline from 05:00 through 06:51, then stepped to ~3.7–4.0 s. The 3-minute-resolution query shows 92.09 ms at 06:51 and 3765.92 ms at 06:54 — a step-change with no gradual ramp. The 10-min query corroborates: last normal bucket 06:40 (88.3 ms), first degraded bucket 06:50 (2288.53 ms avg, 4012.81 max).
auth-service error_rate (HTTP 5xx) was ~0.2% baseline until 06:40, then stepped to ~14%: 0.21% at 06:40, 7.11% (max 14.76%) at 06:50, and 14.12% at 07:00, staying ~13.8–14.1% through 08:50.

The 503 error signature is NOT a downstream timeout or upstream refusal — it is server-side accept-queue exhaustion. All 372 ERROR log entries in 05:00–08:59 are a single pattern: 'request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503 (POST /v1/auth/login)', first seen 06:55:42Z, last 08:58:57Z (result truncated at 30 of 372).

auth-service CPU stepped from a ~38% baseline to ~97%: 38.14% avg (max 40.74) at 06:30, then 69.41% avg (max 97.33) at 06:45 and 97.38% avg at 07:00, pinned high through 08:45 — i.e., the service is CPU-saturated, consistent with the accept-queue-full rejections.

auth-service request_rate roughly tripled/quadrupled at the same onset: ~388–399 req/s baseline through 06:30, then 849.02 avg (max 1813.74) at 06:45 and ~1490–1510 req/s from 07:00 onward, sustained through 08:45.
auth-service did not restart during the window (restarts metric flat at 0.0 for all 240 points, 05:00–08:45), so the degradation is not explained by a crash/restart of auth-service instances.

events.answer: auth-service p99 latency and 5xx errors underwent a step-change (not gradual) at ~06:51–06:54 UTC on 2026-04-22: p99 jumped from a stable ~90 ms baseline to ~3.7–4.0 s and error_rate from ~0.2% to ~14%, with the 503 error signature being "request rejected: accept queue full" on POST /v1/auth/login (server-side accept queue exhaustion, not a downstream timeout). Only auth-service could be fully profiled; blast radius to other services and its dependencies (DB/cache) could not be verified due to tool budget exhaustion.

events.statement: At the onset minute (06:51Z), auth-service request_rate jumped FIRST: 06:50 avg 375.35 req/s, 06:51 avg 529.5, then 715.14 (06:52), 770.48 (06:53), 1012.36 (06:54), and 1813.74 by 06:59 — a monotonic climb starting exactly at 06:51, whereas p99/CPU step-change appears in the 06:48 (cpu) and 06:54 (p99) buckets.

auth-service CPU (6-min buckets) was ~38% through 06:42 (38.49 avg, max 40.45), then rose to 56.79 avg (max 96.96) at 06:48 and 96.74 avg (max 97.33) at 06:54, pinned ~97–99% thereafter — CPU saturation starts within the same bucket as the latency step and follows the request-rate surge, not before it.

auth-service memory_pct stayed flat ~47–57% across the whole onset window (min 46.97, max 57.07, mean 51.99) with no step at 06:51–06:54 — no evidence of a memory/allocation-driven (e.g. bcrypt cost) defect.

user-db CPU stayed flat at ~18% (min 16.25, max 19.99, mean 18.03) through the entire window, but user-db connections_active STEPPED from ~25 to ~76-80 in the 06:52 bucket: 25.02 avg at 06:48, then 76.2 avg (max 79.84) at 06:52, holding ~77-80 through 07:20. The DB connection surge is concurrent with (not before) the auth-side onset and the DB itself shows no CPU stress.

redis-cache (shared by auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service) shows no anomaly at onset: cpu_pct flat ~22% (min 20.15, max 25.59), hit_ratio_pct flat ~96% (min 94.0, max 97.64), evictions_per_min flat ~2-3 (max 4.46). None of its resource metrics move at 06:51–06:54.

Interpretation: neither of auth-service's declared dependencies moved before auth-service did. user-db and redis-cache both show flat/low CPU (18%, 22%) with no pre-onset movement; user-db's connection surge is simultaneous with the auth onset and is consistent with auth-service's own connection pool being filled by the tripled request load, not a DB-side cause. Combined with the flat memory, the pattern is a self-inflicted, load-driven CPU saturation on auth-service (accept-queue full), not a bcrypt-cost regression (which would raise per-request CPU with FLAT request_rate) and not a shared-cache/DB degradation.

events.description: Could not query the auth-service login-path-specific metrics or per-endpoint CPU (no such metric exposed; auth-service available_metrics are only cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, rate_limited_per_min, request_rate, restarts), so I cannot separate bcrypt cost from generic request handling at the endpoint level.

Blast radius to portfolio-service / pricing-engine / market-data-service (the other redis-cache callers, esp. the just-deployed portfolio-service v4.4.0) was not queried in this task's budget, so I cannot confirm whether the request surge originates from portfolio-service's CSV export hitting auth via shared cache or is exogenous.
user-db replication_lag_ms and slow_queries_per_min were available but not queried; redis-cache connected_clients and memory_pct not queried.

events.answer: Latency/errors in auth-service are explained by its OWN behavior — a load-driven CPU saturation: request_rate stepped first at 06:51Z (375→529→1814 req/s by 06:59), auth CPU followed inside the same/next bucket (38%→57%→97%), and memory stayed flat (47–57%). Both dependencies are ruled out as the trigger: user-db CPU flat ~18% (its connection surge at 06:52 is concurrent, not prior) and redis-cache CPU/hit-ratio/evictions all flat (~22%, 96%, ~3). The bcrypt-regression hypothesis (which implies high per-request CPU with FLAT request load, and came from a deployment in HIST-101) is not supported: no auth-service deployment exists, memory is flat, and the request rate — not per-request cost — is what moved. auth-service request_rate moved first among all entities observed.

events.summary: H2's within-auth-service mechanism (load → CPU saturation → accept-queue-full 503s → p99 step) is well grounded by F7/F9/F10/F11/F13/F14, and H2's ordering (request_rate moves first) is verified. H1 and H3 are adequately killed (F15/F11/F13 rule out bcrypt's flat-memory/high-per-request-CPU signature; F16/F17/F18 show no dependency moved first). The blocking gap is the ORIGIN of the surge: H2 asserts it is external and H4 asserts it is portfolio-service dep-5803, and these are the two active hypotheses naming different origins. Neither the blast radius to peer services nor the traffic provenance at the gateway was ever queried (admitted in GAPS and the reasoning agent's own open questions #1–#2). Without that, H4 cannot be dismissed on evidence rather than on the absence of a stated edge. This is obtainable data and could change which hypothesis ranks first. H4 is independently weakened by the 61-minute deploy→onset gap and the flat redis-cache metrics (F17), but not decisively tested.

events.objective: Resolve the origin of the login-traffic surge (H2 external vs H4 portfolio-service dep-5803). At 3-min resolution from 06:30Z-07:30Z, pull request_rate, latency_p99_ms and error_rate for api-gateway, portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service, payment-service and settlement-service. Report whether ANY peer showed a rate/latency/error step or surge at or before 06:51Z, or whether only auth-service moved; specifically portfolio-service request_rate and any auth-token/login call rate in the 05:50-06:51Z window. Then, using api-gateway request_rate plus access-log / per-endpoint breakdown, determine whether the ~4x /v1/auth/login surge originates at the gateway (real end-user/bot traffic) or from an internal service-to-service call pattern beginning ~06:51Z, and report the per-source or per-endpoint split of login traffic. Why: this is the decisive test — if only auth-service moved and the surge is gateway-originated external traffic, H2's external-surge origin stands and H4 is killed; if portfolio-service surged before 06:51Z or the traffic is internal service-to-service, H4 must be re-ranked.

Test the only remaining unmeasured alternate origin (H3 shared-dependency-first) using the metrics never queried: user-db replication_lag_ms and slow_queries_per_min, and redis-cache connected_clients and memory_pct, at 06:30-07:00Z. Did any move before 06:51Z? Why: T3 already showed user-db CPU and redis-cache CPU/hit-ratio/evictions flat, so restrict to these four unmeasured metrics; a move before 06:51Z would revive H3, otherwise H3 is finally killed. Do NOT re-query metrics already tested.

None of the four remaining unmeasured shared-dependency metrics (user-db replication_lag_ms, user-db slow_queries_per_min, redis-cache connected_clients, redis-cache memory_pct) shows any movement before the 06:51Z onset; all four are within tight flat bands through the pre-onset window 06:30–06:50Z. H3 shared-dependency-first is not supported by these metrics.

Same for error_rate: flat ~0.13-0.32% (0.28 at 06:51, 0.19 at 06:54, 0.15 at 07:30; summary max 0.32). No latency or error degradation on the service that carried dep-5803.

events.answer: The login-traffic surge originates at the api-gateway (edge) and is not driven by portfolio-service or any peer: api-gateway request_rate stepped from a flat ~1,261 req/s baseline to 2,102.78 at the 06:51 bucket and climbed to ~4,700-5,200 req/s, while portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service, payment-service and settlement-service all stayed flat across 06:30-07:30. Only auth-service moved at 06:51 (40-50% of gateway traffic). H4 is not supported; the data points to H2 (exogenous edge-originated login surge).

events.title: Exogenous (edge-originated) login request-rate surge saturates auth-service
portfolio-service v4.4.0 CSV-export deployment drives the surge
Shared dependency (user-db/redis-cache) degraded first; auth-service is a downstream victim
Reporter's suspicion: bcrypt cost regression re-introduced (auth-service code)

events.summary: Round 2 resolved the blocking gap I raised: the origin of the surge is now instrumented, not inferred. T4 (F24/F25/F27/F28) shows the api-gateway request_rate stepped +3,500–4,000 req/s in the same 06:51 bucket as auth-service's onset, while portfolio-service (the dep-5803 carrier) and every other peer stayed statistically flat (F25 portfolio 507–618 req/s, min/max/mean across 61 points; F26 latency/error flat; F27 all four peers flat). H4's causal core — portfolio-service generating auth-traffic — is thus contradicted by measurement on both ends: its own request_rate never moved, and no peer contributed any rate increase. H2's within-service mechanism (request_rate first at 06:51 → CPU 38→97% → accept-queue-full 503s → p99 step to ~3.8s) remains verified by F11/F13/F14/F9/F7/F10, with the ordering checked at minute resolution. H1 is dead (no deployment or config in two weeks, F1/F2/F3; flat memory F15; request_rate rose 4x — the opposite of bcrypt's flat-load signature). H3 is dead and re-checked in round 2: the four previously unmeasured shared-dependency metrics (F19/F20/F21/F22) are flat through 06:30–06:50 with no pre-onset movement, and F16's user-db connection step is concurrent, not preceding. One honest residual: the gateway step is only circumstantial proof of the *external/bot* attribution — no per-endpoint/per-source decomposition of gateway traffic to /v1/auth/login was pulled — so "exogenous" is proven in the sense of 'entered above auth-service and not from any measured peer,' but the split between external end-user/bot vs an unmeasured internal caller hitting the login endpoint is inferred. That is a secondary detail of an established origin, not a competing origin, so it caps confidence rather than blocking acceptance. The 61-minute deploy→onset gap and flat redis-cache metrics independently reinforce H4's dismissal. Given the outage is ongoing and remaining rounds cost minutes, further queries are not warranted.

events.why: top hypothesis is above threshold and clearly ahead

tasks.objective: Establish the symptom timeline and true blast radius for the login latency/503 incident. Determine: exact onset time of auth-service p99 degradation and 503s on /v1/auth/login (was it gradual or step-change?); whether other services are also degraded at the same time (latency, error rates, saturation) even if not reported; whether dependencies of auth-service (DB, cache, downstream services) show resource or latency anomalies; and the error signature of the 503s (timeouts, connection pool exhaustion, upstream refused, etc.). Report onset timestamp and the full set of affected services with their metric trends.
tasks.answer: auth-service p99 latency and 5xx errors underwent a step-change (not gradual) at ~06:51–06:54 UTC on 2026-04-22: p99 jumped from a stable ~90 ms baseline to ~3.7–4.0 s and error_rate from ~0.2% to ~14%, with the 503 error signature being "request rejected: accept queue full" on POST /v1/auth/login (server-side accept queue exhaustion, not a downstream timeout). Only auth-service could be fully profiled; blast radius to other services and its dependencies (DB/cache) could not be verified due to tool budget exhaustion.

tasks.objective: Build the change and dependency picture across ALL services around the incident window. List all deployments and config changes (any service, not just auth-service) from ~2026-04-21 through 2026-04-22T08:59Z with timestamps; map auth-service's upstream/downstream dependencies and any shared components (shared cache, DB, auth library); and search historical incidents for the prior bcrypt regression (what its signature and root cause were) plus any other similar login-slowdown precedents. Report which changes plausibly precede the onset and whether the incident pattern matches a code release, a config change, or a shared-infrastructure event.
tasks.answer: No code release and no meaningful config change precedes the onset on auth-service or any dependency: the only deployment in the whole window is portfolio-service v4.4.0 at 2026-04-22T05:50Z (unrelated CSV export), and the only config change is auth-service log.level INFO->WARN at 03:40Z (log volume only). The symptom set is nearly identical to the HIST-101 bcrypt regression (p99 4s, 503 on login, high CPU), but that precedent's cause was a deployment and no auth-service deployment exists now, so the pattern does NOT match a code release; it matches either a shared-infrastructure event (redis-cache is shared and also used by the just-deployed portfolio-service) or an as-yet-unseen cause rather than the bcrypt release the reporter guessed.

tasks.objective: Correlate the change/dependency findings from task b against the onset time found in task a. Specifically test whether latency/errors in auth-service are explained by its own behavior (CPU saturation, bcrypt-like high CPU on login path) versus an external dependency (DB/connection pool, shared cache) by comparing auth-service CPU/memory/latency metrics on the login path with the resource trends of its dependencies at the exact onset time. Confirm or rule out the bcrypt-regression hypothesis and identify which entity moved first.
tasks.answer: Latency/errors in auth-service are explained by its OWN behavior — a load-driven CPU saturation: request_rate stepped first at 06:51Z (375→529→1814 req/s by 06:59), auth CPU followed inside the same/next bucket (38%→57%→97%), and memory stayed flat (47–57%). Both dependencies are ruled out as the trigger: user-db CPU flat ~18% (its connection surge at 06:52 is concurrent, not prior) and redis-cache CPU/hit-ratio/evictions all flat (~22%, 96%, ~3). The bcrypt-regression hypothesis (which implies high per-request CPU with FLAT request load, and came from a deployment in HIST-101) is not supported: no auth-service deployment exists, memory is flat, and the request rate — not per-request cost — is what moved. auth-service request_rate moved first among all entities observed.

tasks.objective: Resolve the origin of the login-traffic surge (H2 external vs H4 portfolio-service dep-5803). At 3-min resolution from 06:30Z-07:30Z, pull request_rate, latency_p99_ms and error_rate for api-gateway, portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service, payment-service and settlement-service. Report whether ANY peer showed a rate/latency/error step or surge at or before 06:51Z, or whether only auth-service moved; specifically portfolio-service request_rate and any auth-token/login call rate in the 05:50-06:51Z window. Then, using api-gateway request_rate plus access-log / per-endpoint breakdown, determine whether the ~4x /v1/auth/login surge originates at the gateway (real end-user/bot traffic) or from an internal service-to-service call pattern beginning ~06:51Z, and report the per-source or per-endpoint split of login traffic. Why: this is the decisive test — if only auth-service moved and the surge is gateway-originated external traffic, H2's external-surge origin stands and H4 is killed; if portfolio-service surged before 06:51Z or the traffic is internal service-to-service, H4 must be re-ranked.
tasks.answer: The login-traffic surge originates at the api-gateway (edge) and is not driven by portfolio-service or any peer: api-gateway request_rate stepped from a flat ~1,261 req/s baseline to 2,102.78 at the 06:51 bucket and climbed to ~4,700-5,200 req/s, while portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service, payment-service and settlement-service all stayed flat across 06:30-07:30. Only auth-service moved at 06:51 (40-50% of gateway traffic). H4 is not supported; the data points to H2 (exogenous edge-originated login surge).

tasks.objective: Test the only remaining unmeasured alternate origin (H3 shared-dependency-first) using the metrics never queried: user-db replication_lag_ms and slow_queries_per_min, and redis-cache connected_clients and memory_pct, at 06:30-07:00Z. Did any move before 06:51Z? tasks.answer: No — none of the four previously-unmeasured shared-dependency metrics moved before 06:51Z. user-db replication_lag_ms (flat ~30 ms) and slow_queries_per_min (flat ~0.3/min), and redis-cache connected_clients (flat ~309) and memory_pct (flat ~70%) all stayed within tight bands across 06:30–07:00Z with no step at or before the 06:51Z onset. H3 shared-dependency-first is not revived and can be considered killed by these metrics.

critiques.summary: H2's within-auth-service mechanism (load → CPU saturation → accept-queue-full 503s → p99 step) is well grounded by F7/F9/F10/F11/F13/F14, and H2's ordering (request_rate moves first) is verified. H1 and H3 are adequately killed (F15/F11/F13 rule out bcrypt's flat-memory/high-per-request-CPU signature; F16/F17/F18 show no dependency moved first). The blocking gap is the ORIGIN of the surge: H2 asserts it is external and H4 asserts it is portfolio-service dep-5803, and these are the two active hypotheses naming different origins. Neither the blast radius to peer services nor the traffic provenance at the gateway was ever queried (admitted in GAPS and the reasoning agent's own open questions #1–#2). Without that, H4 cannot be dismissed on evidence rather than on the absence of a stated edge. This is obtainable data and could change which hypothesis ranks first. H4 is independently weakened by the 61-minute deploy→onset gap and the flat redis-cache metrics (F17), but not decisively tested.

challenges.issue: The claim 'something EXTERNAL to auth-service multiplied inbound login rate' is an unverified assumption. No peer-service or gateway traffic metrics were pulled, so the surge's origin (exogenous client/bot vs internal caller) is untested — yet it is the only distinguishing feature vs H4.

Was not decisively tested: no portfolio-service, redis-cache caller, or gateway metrics were queried. It is dismissed largely on the absence of a stated edge plus flat redis-cache (F17), while its stated mechanism (lagging export loop over 61 min) remains unfalsified.
Autoscaling/replica-count behavior for auth-service is untracked; the 'capacity adequate for baseline but not 4x' claim rests on flat restarts (F12), which is indirect.

user-db replication_lag_ms / slow_queries_per_min and redis-cache connected_clients were available but never queried; the rule-out rests on CPU/hit-ratio/evictions only. Secondary detail, unlikely to flip ranking.

critiques.summary: Round 2 resolved the blocking gap I raised: the origin of the surge is now instrumented, not inferred. T4 (F24/F25/F27/F28) shows the api-gateway request_rate stepped +3,500–4,000 req/s in the same 06:51 bucket as auth-service's onset, while portfolio-service (the dep-5803 carrier) and every other peer stayed statistically flat (F25 portfolio 507–618 req/s, min/max/mean across 61 points; F26 latency/error flat; F27 all four peers flat). H4's causal core — portfolio-service generating auth-traffic — is thus contradicted by measurement on both ends: its own request_rate never moved, and no peer contributed any rate increase. H2's within-service mechanism (request_rate first at 06:51 → CPU 38→97% → accept-queue-full 503s → p99 step to ~3.8s) remains verified by F11/F13/F14/F9/F7/F10, with the ordering checked at minute resolution. H1 is dead (no deployment or config in two weeks, F1/F2/F3; flat memory F15; request_rate rose 4x — the opposite of bcrypt's flat-load signature). H3 is dead and re-checked in round 2: the four previously unmeasured shared-dependency metrics (F19/F20/F21/F22) are flat through 06:30–06:50 with no pre-onset movement, and F16's user-db connection step is concurrent, not preceding. One honest residual: the gateway step is only circumstantial proof of the *external/bot* attribution — no per-endpoint/per-source decomposition of gateway traffic to /v1/auth/login was pulled — so "exogenous" is proven in the sense of 'entered above auth-service and not from any measured peer,' but the split between external end-user/bot vs an unmeasured internal caller hitting the login endpoint is inferred. That is a secondary detail of an established origin, not a competing origin, so it caps confidence rather than blocking acceptance. The 61-minute deploy→onset gap and flat redis-cache metrics independently reinforce H4's dismissal. Given the outage is ongoing and remaining rounds cost minutes, further queries are not warranted.

challenges.issue: The 'exogenous/edge-originated' label is inferred from magnitude and the gateway-vs-peers contrast (F24/F28), not from traffic provenance. No per-endpoint or per-source split of the api-gateway surge was obtained, so an unmeasured internal caller hitting /v1/auth/login directly could in principle produce the same gateway step. This is a labeling uncertainty on an otherwise established origin (surge entered above auth-service, no peer moved), not a competing origin.

No autoscaling/replica-count evidence (F12 flat restarts is only indirect), so the sub-claim 'no auth-service fault; capacity merely inadequate for ~1500 req/s' rests on an untracked assumption. This affects the mitigation narrative, not the causal origin or ranking.

Rejection is now evidence-based (F25/F26/F27 flat on portfolio-service and all peers; F24 gateway-only step) but the deploy→onset 61-minute gap remains unexplained by any positive mechanism, so H4 is dismissed rather than positively explained away.

Killed on resource metrics (F17/F19/F20/F21/F22) and ordering (F13/F16); a non-resource shared-path failure (network/route/config on the shared dependency path) would be invisible to these six metrics. Low residual risk given the accept-queue-full server-side signature and request_rate leading.
